at.step: An orchestrator holds four thousand tasks, two hundred of them ready to run, and thirty-two free worker slots. Which thirty-two run first decides how long the whole pipeline takes. By default, Airflow gives each task a weight equal to its own weight plus the weight of everything below it, so the task with the most things below it goes first. Predict: for a task with a three-task chain below it and a task with a five-task fan-out below it, which does the default rule run first, and which one finishes the pipeline sooner?

Kahn's algorithm, the textbook underneath every scheduler: each task starts with an in-degree, the count of unfinished upstream tasks. A task is ready the moment its in-degree reaches zero. Pop a ready task, decrement its children's in-degree, and push any child that just reached zero. Nothing here is new; a real scheduler's graph is simply live, not static.

The chapter's own DAG, drawn left to right by duration: a critical chain of four tasks, a wide fan-out off a separate head task, and a second, narrower chain that runs longer than either. Fourteen tasks in all, two workers, exactly the shape the rest of this topic measures.

Airflow's own documentation, read at research time: priority_weight defines priorities in the executor queue, defaults to one, and can be bumped to any integer. By default, the weighting method is downstream, described in the same page as the aggregate sum of all downstream descendants.

at.deep: A weight computed once, not recomputed per step

at.step: The exact formula, read from priority_strategy.py: a task's own weight plus the weight of every id returned by get_flat_relative_ids with upstream set to false. That method returns a set of strings, read from node.py, so a descendant reachable by two different routes is counted once, never once per route.

The prediction, measured: the chain's own head task carries a default weight of four; the fan-out's head carries six. Scheduled on two workers, the fan-out starts first, exactly as the rule predicts. Yet the chain's own last task finishes at the same step either way: ten.

Set each task's priority_weight to its own duration instead of one, and the same formula becomes a sum over descendant durations, not descendant counts. The chain's head now carries ten, ahead of the fan-out's six: this is what a user reaching for a critical-path order actually has to do, since Airflow has no separate critical-path rule.

Add the second, narrower chain competing for the same two workers, and the two rules genuinely diverge. The plain count-based rule still finishes the watched chain's last task at ten. The duration-weighted rule, measured on this exact DAG, finishes it at eleven: worse, not better. One measured DAG, not a general claim about either rule.

With no worker limit at all, the makespan is exactly the critical path: the longest chain of summed durations through the whole graph. On this DAG that longest chain runs through the narrower distractor, not the chain the rest of this topic has been watching, and it finishes later than that watched chain ever does alone.

Graham's bound, proved for any list-scheduling order under a fixed worker count: the makespan is at most two minus one over the worker count, times the true optimum. Both measured schedules on this DAG, default and duration-weighted alike, land well inside that bound: a guarantee that holds regardless of which ready task a rule picks first.

A planted edge closes a cycle in the chapter's own DAG. Kahn's algorithm, run to the end, leaves a set of tasks whose in-degree never reaches zero. Airflow's own detect_cycle, an iterative three-colour depth-first search, instead tracks the exact path it is currently following. Predict: when the cycle is found, which of the two names the single edge that closes the loop, and which only shows the whole stuck group?
